42. It was held that the Company was commercially insolvent and a winding up order should be passed. In this case the legal connotation of the term "commercially insolvent" given as follows by Sir William James, V.C. In Re European Life Assurance Society, (1869) 9 Eq 122 was cited and relied on: 

 43.  In A.I.R. 1942 Bom. 231, In re Cine Industries and Recording Co. Ltd. which was also referred to by both sides the petition for winding up was filed by (a share-holder holding 5 shares out of 1966 shares and not a single creditor supported his petition. It was held by Chagla, J in his learned discussion that the mere fact that the petitioner holding only 5 shares should not prevent the Court from making the winding up order but in coming to that Conclusion Court should keep in consideration mainly the interest of both the share-holders and the creditors and the fact that the overwhelming majority of the share-holders are opposing the petition and a large number of creditors are also doing the same and the rest are taking no part IS a fact which must bear with the Court in coming to the decision. The learned Judge also referred to the expression "commercially insolvent" as defined in (1869) 9 Eq. 122, In re European Life Assurance Society and to A.I.R. 1936 P.c. 114, Davis V. Brunswick (Supra) and held that it is for the petitioner to satisfy the Court that there IS no reasonable hope that the object of trading at a profit, with a view to which the Company was formed can be attained. The learned Judge following (1867) 2 Ch. A.737. In re Suburban Hotel Co observed that the petition seemed to have been presented for the object of evoking judicial decisions as to the probable success or non-success of the Company as a commercial speculation, and refused to give any decision thereon. 

 45. There is another important fact to be borne in mind. This is a share-holder's petition. It is true that as the law stands today, he is under no disability as compares with a contributory nor is he under any obligation, as he at one time was, to satisfy the Court that on a winding up there would!' be surplus assets. But there is a special rule that the courts have laid down in exercising their discretion in winding up a company on the petition of a share-holder. The Court constantly bears in mind that the internal management of the Company is its own concern, and it is a much better judge of business prospect of a trading venture than the court can ever hope to be. If, therefore, the majority of the share-holders show confidence in the management of the company and have faith in its future prospects, the court has rarely interfered. In 39 Boom 16, Macleod, J. Stated that a share-holder's petition must be scrutinized much more carefully than, a contributory's. In (1867) 2 Ch. A 737, In re Suburban Hotel Co., Cairns L.J. refused to wind up the Company against the wishes of the majority of the share-holders of the Company because the business had been carried on at a loss and appeared likely to continue as a losing concern. In (1871) Ch. A. 641, In re London Suburban Bank, the great body of share-holders were opposed to a winding up, and there too the order as refused. The principle of these decisions is well stated in (1880) 14 Ch. D. 104, where James, L.J. stated (Page 109): 

 "Another rule which the Court follows is that if there is opposition to the making of the winding up order by the creditors the Court will consider their wishes and may decline to make winding up order. Under s. 557 of the Companies Act, in all matters relating to the winding up of the Company the Court may ascertain the wishes of the creditors. The wishes of the shareholders are also considered though perhaps the Court may attach greater weight to the views of the creditors. The law on this point is stated in Palmer's Company Law., 21st Edition, page 742 as follows "This right to a winding up order is however, qualified by another rule, viz. that the Court will regard the wishes of majority in value of the creditors, and if for some good reason, they object to a winding up order, the Court in its discretion map refuse the Order" (page 2605) Held further : "In determining whether or not the substratum of the Company has gone, the objects of the Company and the case of the Company on that question will have to be locked into. In the present case the Company alleged that with the proceeds of sale the company intended to enter into some other profitable business. The mere fact that the Company has suffered trading losses will not destroy its substratum unless there is no reasonable prospect of it ever (under lining is mine) making a profit in future, and the Court is reluctant to hold that it has no such prospect. (See Re Suburban Hotel Co. (1867) 2Ch. A 737 and Davis & Co. V. Brunswick, (1936) 1 All E.R. 299 (page 2607). 

 66. Under the 1st ground, namely, inability to pay its debts, petitioners case is based not on any current demands actually made by a creditor and the Company has not paid that or is unable to pay that, but is based on the existing state of liabilities of the Company which, according to the petitioners, the Company existing and probable assets are insufficient to meet, that is, the Company is Commercially insolvent (in re European Life Assurance Society, (1869) X.. R. 9 Eq. 122 (128). In considering the question of commercial insolvency the Court will have to take into. account the second ground as well, whether it would be just and equitable to wind up the Company and for that purpose amongst others the question whether at the date of the presentation of the winding up petition there was any reasonable hope that the object of trading at a profit, with a view to which the Company was formed could be attained (A.LR. 1936) P.C. 114 D. Davis Co. Ltd. V. Brunswick Ltd.). 

 "The principle laid down by Lord Cairns in In re Suburban Hotel Co. (1867) 2 Ch. Ap.737. that it is not permissible to argue from the mere fact that company has consistently made losses in the past that it has no reasonable prospects of earning profits in the future has been repeatedly affirmed and the decision itself has been taken to have established the fact that a company "has lost, is lose and will continue to lose" docs not of itself justify winding up order, at least when the capital has not been exhausted".(page 248). 

 89. In this connection reference may also be made to A.I.R. 1942 Bom. 231, In re line Industries and Recording Co. Ltd. (Supra), where Chagla, J, as his Lordship then was held that a share-holder is not under any obligation to satisfy the Court that on a winding up there would be surplus assets. But there is a special rule that the Courts have laid down in exercising their discretion in winding up on the petition of a share-holder, namely, that the internal management of the Company is own concern, and it is a much better judge of business prospects of a trading venture than the Court can ever hope to be. If, therefore the majority of share-holders show confidence in the management of the company and have faith in its future prospects, the Court has rarely interfered.
